### C-R8-01
**Claim:** Part 3c (Jer 34–36) completes the concentric frame around Jeremiah’s “book of hope” by reversing temporal setting from Zedekiah’s tenth year (final siege) back to Jehoiakim’s fourth year; after promissory Jer 30–33, the scroll returns to “reality” with gloomy stories.
**Quote:** “So Jer 34–36 as a whole completes ‘the concentric frame around Jeremiah’s book of hope by reversing the temporal setting from the tenth year of Zedekiah during the final siege of Jerusalem back to the fourth year of Jehoiakim.’” / “We are ‘back to reality.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 1–25 (Part 3c intro; units 34:1–7; 34:8–22; 35:1–19; 36:1–32)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-02
**Claim:** In Jer 34:1–7 Goldingay reads Yahweh’s threat-and-promise to Zedekiah as ambiguous challenge, not inevitability: capture and eye-to-eye meeting with the Babylonian king are certain-sounding, yet “you will not die by the sword; in peace you will die” functions as conditional challenge depending on response; fulfillment involves irony (39:5–7; 52:9–11) and unresolved questions about how Zedekiah died.
**Quote:** “As well as being ambiguous, they are not statements about what will inevitably happen. They constitute a challenge to respond.” / “You will not die by the sword; in peace you will die is thus a ‘syntactical chiasm.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 35–113 (34:1–7 translation + commentary vv. 1–7)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-03
**Claim:** 34:6–7 situates the message before the city’s final siege, with Babylon focusing on Lachish and Azekah; Goldingay links this to Lachish ostraca (one possibly reporting inability to see Azekah’s fire signals) and treats audience after 587 as already knowing Zedekiah’s choices.
**Quote:** “We have a collection of ostraca from Lachish that apparently come from just before the fall of that city and of Jerusalem itself and thus from 589/588.” / “one mentions being unable to see fire signals from Azekah, which might mean that Azekah has fallen.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 110–113 (commentary vv. 6–7)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-04
**Claim:** Jer 34:8–22 narrates Zedekiah’s covenant-proclamation of release (dĕrôr) for Hebrew bondservants, then reneging when Babylon temporarily withdraws; Yahweh’s indictment links the act to Sinai/Egypt release, six/seven-year manumission traditions (Exod 21 / Deut 15 / Lev 25 blended), and covenant-cutting (calf split, Gen 15 analogy).
**Quote:** “Zedekiah’s action does not correspond to any single formulation in the Torah.” / “They overstepped my pledge? … a calf that they cut into two and passed between the parts.” / “Apparently, it was this relief that stimulated the householders to go back on the release of the bondservants.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 117–253 (34:8–22 translation + commentary)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-05
**Claim:** The punishment fits the crime: because they failed to proclaim release, Yahweh proclaims a “release” of them to sword, epidemic, and hunger; he will turn the Babylonians back to take and burn the city (34:17–22). The story explains the fall for a post-587 audience.
**Quote:** “You have pulled back from proclaiming a release? Okay, here am I, proclaiming a release to you: the punishment will fit the crime.” / “vv. 21–22 are its climax.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 249–253
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-06
**Claim:** Jer 35 pairs with 34:8–22 as fidelity vs. infidelity: Rechabites keep Jonadab’s ancestral orders (no wine, no houses/vineyards/fields; tent life) for over two centuries, while Judah ignores Yahweh’s prophetic word; Goldingay stresses a fortiori contrast, not endorsement of Rechabite lifestyle as ideal for all.
**Quote:** “It makes an a fortiori contrast between people who would live by their ancestor’s word and people who would not even live by their God’s word.” / “Yahweh does not imply that the Rechabites’ lifestyle is preferable to the regular Judahite lifestyle… Yahweh’s point is rather that they did what they were bidden to do.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 259–447 (35:1–19 + commentary, esp. 316–328, 441–447)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-07
**Claim:** Rechabite presence in Jerusalem is tied to Nebuchadrezzar’s advance (~600, 2 Kgs 24:1–2 context); promise that Jonadab will not lack someone “standing before me” is a parody of Davidic/Levitical promises (33:17–22); Second Temple data on Rechabites is thin (Neh 3:14; m. Taʿanit 4:5).
**Quote:** “Thus he gives them a ‘parody’ of his promise to David and to the Levites (see 33:17–22)—as if they were as important as them!” / “There was infinitely more hope for this fringe group than for mainstream Judaism.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 439–447
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Priority: Scroll burned (Jer 36) and 604 / “point of no return”

### C-R8-08
**Claim:** Jer 36 pairs with Jer 25 as same-year event (fourth year of Jehoiakim), pairs with Jer 45 by date, completes the Jer 26–36 chiasm, and “faces both ways”: decisions in Jehoiakim’s day bear fruit over the next twenty years into Jer 37–44.
**Quote:** “It also relates to the same year as Jer 25 and pairs with it in its historical significance.” / “the chapter forms a pair with Jer 45, which bears the same date.” / “it leads into Jer 37–44 by suggesting how decisions taken in Jehoiakim’s day bore their dire fruit over the next twenty years.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 534–536
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-09
**Claim:** Goldingay dates Jer 36 to the key Western-Asian year when Nebuchadrezzar became king of Babylon and won significant victories (cross-ref Jer 25:1–2); Yahweh’s commission to write all words from Josiah’s days onward aims at possible turning and pardon—“Perhaps the household of Judah may listen.”
**Quote:** “Jeremiah 36 relates to a key year in the history of Western Asia, the year Nebuchadrezzar became king of Babylon and won significant military victories.” / “Perhaps is a natural word… Here, it again comes on Yahweh’s lips… the future really is open.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 536; 772–776 (vv. 1–3 commentary)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

**Quote:** “one of the great narratives, not only of the book of Jeremiah but also in the whole Bible.” / five-act outline (Acts 1–5, vv. 1–32)
**Locus:** slice ll. 536–674
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

**Claim:** Baruch is first known contact with Jeremiah in this commission (Jer 32 chronologically later); Jeremiah is “under restraint” (house arrest/custody), so Baruch writes and reads; purpose of public reading is prayer for grace and turning from a dire path.

**Locus:** slice ll. 778–786
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-12

**Quote:** “So the fast happens in the month the Babylonians sacked Ashkelon, forty miles away, though we don’t know if the audience could be expected to know about that collocation of dates.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 788–800 (v. 9 commentary + Chronicle quote)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-13
**Claim:** Shaphan family (Gemariah’s room) is sympathetic platform for the reading; officials fear and want to tell the king, quiz Baruch, deposit scroll with Elishama, and urge Baruch and Jeremiah to hide—caught between Jeremiah and Jehoiakim (Elnathan had extradited Uriah, 26:20–23).

### C-R8-14
**Claim:** Jehoiakim burns the scroll piece by piece (three or four columns at a time) with a scribe’s knife into a winter-house brazier—cold, systematic rejection, not impulsive rage; burning is Jehoiakim’s symbolic act paralleling Hananiah’s (Jer 28) and inverting Josiah’s burning of cult objects.

### C-R8-15
**Claim:** Jer 36 is an “upside-down” Josiah story (2 Kgs 22–23): king rips scroll not clothes; no fear; arrest of prophet not consultation; disaster not well-being promised; Jehoiakim as anti-Josiah is one-word answer to how things went so wrong after Josiah.
**Quote:** “one significance of the Jehoiakim story is that he appears as an anti-Josiah. Josiah is not his father.” / “how could things have gone so wrong when they seemed to be going so right a few decades ago? The one-word answer is Jehoiakim.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 682–768 (comparison table + conclusion)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-16
**Claim (604 / point of no return):** Burning does not forestall judgment; it seals it. Goldingay (with cited scholars) treats the ashes under the brazier as determining Judah’s fate by end of Part III; Jehoiakim’s act “releases the fatal word” / makes doom “ineluctable”; “Within a brief period of four years, Jehoiakim’s regime nails the coffin shut on the Judean nation.” No šûb in the tragic conclusion.
**Quote:** “By the end of Part III the fate of Jerusalem and Judah is determined by the ashes of that scroll lying under the king’s brazier…. The king may burn the scroll, but he cannot prevent its contents becoming operative”; indeed, it is his symbolic act that “releases the fatal word.” / “by burning the original scroll, Jehoiakim … has ironically unleashed the threatened doom upon himself and the nation as their ineluctable fate.” / “Within a brief period of four years, Jehoiakim’s regime nails the coffin shut on the Judean nation.” / “ominously there is no reference to repentance (šûb) as there was in the initial scene.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 814–818 (vv. 27–31 commentary)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-17
**Claim:** Yahweh commissions rewrite; extra threat: Jehoiakim will not have someone sitting on David’s throne; corpse thrown out to heat/cold; personal threats not to be taken too literally (son briefly succeeds; 2 Kgs 24:6 death account differs). **Quote:** “Jeremiah rewrites the scroll, sealing Jehoiakim’s judgment.” / “There was also added to them many words like them.” / “Maybe… Jer 2–6 goes back to the scroll whose origins this story tells. It’s a guess, but it makes sense.”

## Part 4 overview (37:1–45:5)

### C-R8-20
**Claim:** Part Four is semi-continuous narrative of ~four–five years (589/588–585+) from pre-fall through fall to Judah/Egypt aftermath; themes: ask Jeremiah then ignore him; constraints yet survival; word comes true; Babylon as agent yet merciful if cooperative; Egyptian Judahites without hope; “choice and destiny.”
**Quote:** “Part Four comprises a semi-continuous series of stories relating to a crucial period of four or five years between 589/588 and 585.” / listed themes including “The disobedience of the Judahite community in Egypt means there is no hope for it.” / “Events reflect the interweaving of ‘choice and destiny.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 1847–1864
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-21
**Claim:** Narrative may have been developed in Egypt; practical implications include accept deserved calamity, stay firm if messenger, respond to Yahweh, submit to imperial authority rather than rebel. Goldingay resists reading the Egypt-dismissive narrative primarily as Babylonian-Judahite polemic against Egyptian Jews.
**Quote:** “So it requires considerable connecting of dots to suppose that (e.g.) Judahites who had been in Babylon composed this narrative to discredit Judahites in Egypt.” / “Maybe Judahites in Egypt could write self-critically.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 1866–1880
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

Jeremiah chooses Gedaliah—validating ongoing community; Shaphan family continuum (Ahikam 26:24; 2 Kgs 22).

## Priority: Flight to Egypt (42–44)

### C-R8-37
**Claim:** At Bethlehem, entire company asks Jeremiah to plead/inquire for path and deed; swear to do whatever Yahweh says (good or dire). After ten days: if stay in land—build/plant, not smash/pull up; Yahweh has relented over the dire thing; don’t fear Babylon; compassion from Yahweh and from king of Babylon, return to land. If go to Egypt—sword/hunger/epidemic there; wrath as on Jerusalem; become oath/desolation; not see this place again.
**Quote:** “Whereas Jeremiah had once told people not to stay where they are if they want to have a future (38:2), now he tells the remaining Judahites to stay where they are if they want to have a future.” / “I have relented over the dire thing that I did to you.” / “He sets two paths before them… the path to life and the path to death.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 2850–2998 (42:1–18)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-38
**Claim:** Relenting (nāḥam) here means intention not to destroy again if they stay—not unconditional; 24:6 build/plant language now applies even to “dire figs” who remain. Fear of Babylon addressed three times; empire can be agent of compassion.

### C-R8-41
**Claim:** Whole remainder—including king’s daughters, Jeremiah, and Baruch—goes to Tahpanhes (NE Egyptian border fortress). Why take the two? ## Priority: Baruch promise (45)

### C-R8-46
**Claim:** Jer 45 is second coda: word to Baruch when he wrote “these words” from dictation in Jehoiakim’s fourth year—same 604 horizon as Jer 36/25; “these words” not ch. 44 and not simply ch. 36 scroll; answer emerges at 46:1–2 (oracles against nations). Placement odd chronologically but theologically loaded after Egypt narrative.
**Quote:** “A message for Baruch forms a second coda to the narrative in Jer 37–43.” / “In light of the date that follows, they cannot be the preceding words in Jer 44. And in light of the big gap since Jer 36, they can hardly be the words that Baruch took down that year… The answer to the question will emerge only in 46:1–2.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 3506–3520
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-47
**Claim:** Connections of placement: with 43:3 (Baruch blamed); with 42:10 build/plant language inverted to smash/pull up; with 39:15–18 Ebed-melech (life as loot); “places you go” illumined by Egypt—Yahweh kept word ~20 years.
**Quote:** “Located here, however, vv. 2–3 suggest a link with the nearer narrative at 43:3.” / “the last phrase in v. 5, referring to places where Baruch might have to go, is now illumined by the fact that he is in Egypt. Yahweh has kept his word for twenty years so far.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 3508–3516
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-48
**Claim:** Baruch’s complaint (psalm-like): Yahweh added suffering to pain; weary with groaning; no relief—hendiadys of piled anguish; may voice people’s anguish (604 anticipatory; placement = post-disaster + Jer 44 further suffering), not only personal danger. Yahweh’s first response: “Tough”—what I built I smash, planted I pull up (entire country). Second: don’t seek big things (prayer for restoration-scale promises; none of part-3 restoration hope in part 4). Third: life as loot wherever he goes.
**Quote:** “So whereas you for yourself, you seek big things—don’t seek them, because here am I, letting something dire come upon all flesh… But I am giving you your life as loot in all the places that you go to.” / “There are no great promises of restoration in part 4 of the Jeremiah scroll like the ones in part 3.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 3522–3528
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R8-49
**Claim:** “All flesh” / “entire country” may also open onto the nations (Jer 46–51); like 25 and 36, ch. 45 faces both ways—end of narrative and beginning of oracles against nations. Message not merely private: testifies to cost paid by secretary as well as messenger; humble scribal role, not generative author of prophetic content.
**Quote:** “Like Jer 25 and Jer 36, it is both an end and a beginning. It faces both ways.” / “it does not suggest that he or scribes like him were the kind of people who generated the content of a prophetic scroll.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 3518–3528
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Additional structural / hermeneutical claims

### C-R8-50
**Claim:** Across 34–36 and 37–45 Goldingay repeatedly stresses: stories function for post-587 audiences (Mizpah/Egypt); dramatic rather than purely chronological order; MT often longer than LXX (haplography vs. expansion debates); threats/promises as challenges with real human freedom; Babylon as Yahweh’s servant/agent whose selfishness God harnesses.
**Quote:** “The empire is always selfish, but God sometimes harnesses its selfishness.” (34:22 context) / “What happens issues from Yahweh and his decisions; it also issues from Nebuchadrezzar and his decisions.” (43:12)
